questions.explain: Kubernetes is the right home for ephemeral workloads (dev/test per pull request, CI disposable databases) and identical environments across clouds; it's the wrong home when you need the highest availability with the least effort, don't already operate Kubernetes, or need every last IOPS.
options: Production OLTP needing maximum IOPS
Ephemeral workloads like dev/test per pull request and CI disposable databases
Teams new to Kubernetes wanting the easiest HA
Workloads that must avoid all container overhead
questions.q: When is Kubernetes the right home for SQL Server, per the chapter?

questions.explain: SQL Server runs as a StatefulSet with one SQL Server per pod, one pod per node (anti-affinity), each pod with a PersistentVolumeClaim on SSD-backed storage; the database files live on the persistent volume while the image holds only binaries.
options: A Deployment with ephemeral local storage
A StatefulSet — one SQL Server per pod, anti-affinity, PersistentVolumeClaim on SSD-backed storage
A DaemonSet on every node
A single container with no persistent volume
questions.q: What is the chapter's recommended Kubernetes deployment pattern for SQL Server?

questions.explain: For AGs across pods, the availability group listener becomes a Kubernetes Service; failover orchestration, quorum, and health probing are your responsibility — AGs in Kubernetes are real but manual.
options: The listener becomes a ClusterIP for SQL Browser
The availability group listener becomes a Kubernetes Service, with failover orchestration and quorum as your responsibility
AGs are not possible in Kubernetes
The listener is replaced by an Ingress rule
questions.q: How do Always On availability groups across SQL Server pods expose their listener, per the chapter?

questions.explain: SQL Server's memory model (max server memory) must fit inside the container's memory limit with headroom for the OS — an OOM-killed SQL Server pod is an avoidable outage. Set CPU and memory requests/limits deliberately.
options: Max server memory must fit inside the container's memory limit with headroom for the OS
Memory limits are ignored by SQL Server
Requests must exceed node capacity
Only CPU limits matter
questions.q: What resource-limit rule does the chapter give for SQL Server pods?

questions.explain: The chapter is explicit: a SQL Server exposed to the internet via a public load balancer is an incident waiting to happen. Keep the load balancer internal and use private VPC IPs.
options: Use a public load balancer for easier access
Expose port 1433 with an internet gateway
Keep the load balancer internal on a private VPC IP — a public-facing SQL Server is an incident waiting to happen
Use NodePort for all external clients
questions.q: How should external clients reach SQL Server on Kubernetes, per the chapter?
